page: Microsoft Azure E16pds_v7 is an ARM-based virtual machine within the memory-optimized family, running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. The instance is configured with 16 dedicated ARM64 vCPUs and 128 GB of system memory, establishing an 8:1 memory-to-core ratio of 8.0 GB RAM per vCPU. It bundles 944 GB of local NVMe SSD storage for fast local data access. The instance does not include discrete GPU hardware and offers zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

The use of dedicated ARM64 cores provides consistent execution threads alongside resource density benefits. The integrated 944 GB NVMe SSD delivers low-latency scratch space and temporary file capabilities directly on the host node, avoiding network storage latency for ephemeral data. A natural operational tradeoff stems from the ARM64 architecture, which necessitates compatible operating systems and application binaries, precluding workloads that depend on specialized x86 instruction sets.

Given its high memory-per-core density and bundled high-speed local NVMe disk, the E16pds_v7 is structured for memory-heavy enterprise deployments. Primary workload fits include in-memory key-value stores, distributed memory caches, enterprise relational databases, large-scale ETL pipelines, and memory-intensive data processing jobs.
description: The Microsoft Azure E16pds_v7 is a memory-optimized virtual machine built on 16 dedicated ARM64 vCPUs and 128 GB of RAM, providing an 8 GB per core memory profile. The ARM64 processor architecture delivers compute efficiency and reliable resource isolation via dedicated core allocations. The integrated NVMe storage eliminates external disk latency for ephemeral data access, though the platform requires ARM-compatible software builds and lacks x86-specific instruction support. With its substantial memory density and fast local disk, the E16pds_v7 is designed for memory-intensive workloads, including in-memory key-value stores, distributed caches, enterprise relational databases, big data batch processing, and memory-constrained ETL workloads.
